Sample text:
---
### In Praise of Lingering

There is an art to lingering, and we're losing it.

Not loitering, exactly. Not wasting time, either — though from the outside they can look identical. Lingering is what happens when you stay a little longer than necessary, for no good reason except that the moment hasn't quite finished with you yet.

It's the old man on the park bench who has finished his sandwich but stays to watch the pigeons sort out their complicated social hierarchy. It's staying in the bookshop after you've already found the book you came for, just to read first pages you have no intention of buying. It's the last ten minutes of a dinner party, when the coats are on and everyone is standing by the door, and somehow that's when the best conversation of the whole night happens.

We are very good now at arriving and departing. We optimize the in-between. We listen at 1.5x speed, we skim to the summary, we take the photo and move to the next viewpoint before we've really looked at the first one. Efficiency is a wonderful servant, but it is a terrible guide for how to live a day.

Lingering is inefficient on purpose.

I love the moment just after rain, when the pavement is dark and shining and the air smells like wet earth and hot stone. Nothing is happening, technically. The storm is over. You could go inside. But if you stand there for thirty seconds longer, you notice how every leaf is holding one perfect drop, and how quiet the street gets, as if the whole neighborhood is also standing still, listening.

I love museum closing time, when the crowds thin out and the guard in the last room isn't rushing you, and you finally look — really look — at the painting in the corner that nobody photographs. The one of a table, set for supper, with the bread already torn. Someone lived there, once, in the painter's mind, anyway. Someone was about to sit down.

I love train stations late at night. Not the big departures, but the pauses between them. The echo of your own footsteps. A vending machine humming to itself. A stranger asleep with their head on their backpack, trusting the world not to bother them for a while. For a few minutes, a place designed entirely for going somewhere becomes a place just to *be* somewhere.

Maybe that's the secret. Lingering turns transit into inhabiting.

Children understand this instinctively. A walk to school that should take ten minutes takes forty because there is a particularly interesting stick, a puddle that needs investigating, a cat that must be negotiated with. Adults call it dawdling. Children would call it, if they had the word, paying attention.

And attention, I've come to think, is a form of affection. What we linger over, we love a little. Not always grandly. Sometimes just enough to learn its details: the chip in your favorite mug, the way light hits your kitchen at 6:42 in the morning in October, the exact sound a friend makes when they're about to laugh before they actually do.

The world will keep rewarding us for moving faster. It will give us points and badges and saved seconds. It will not, very often, reward us for standing in a doorway a moment longer to finish a thought, or for taking the long way home because the long way passes the bakery and the street with the jasmine spilling over the fence.

But life, inconveniently, doesn't happen at the destinations. It happens in the doorway. In the pause between songs. In the extra minute by the window.

So linger, when you can. Let the tea go a little cool while you finish the paragraph. Stay for the credits. Watch the pigeons settle their arguments. You won't get that time back, of course.

That's rather the point.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical, sensory essay turns an everyday preference into a gently argued way of living.

## Grounded reading
The voice is warm and observant, finding emotional weight in small pauses: rain-dark pavement, a nearly empty museum, a late-night station, a mug’s chip. Its pathos is quiet rather than nostalgic; it suggests that ordinary moments are easy to miss when life is organized around speed and destinations. The reader is invited not to accomplish more, but to notice and stay a little longer.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds lingering as deliberate inefficiency, attention as a form of affection, and the value of inhabiting transitions rather than hurrying through them. Its recurring objects and scenes—pigeons, doorways, train stations, tea, light, and a bakery on the long way home—make that claim tangible. The closing turn treats lost time not as a cost to recover but as the point.

## Evidence line
> Lingering is inefficient on purpose.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The coherent voice, recurring sensory details, and consistent moral emphasis make this a distinctive sample rather than a generic case for slowing down.
